items.description: Analyze repository structure, existing algorithm implementations (Dijkstra, A*, BALT-H), benchmark infrastructure, and test suite to understand the codebase foundation
items.acceptance_criteria: Written document listing all modules (src/graph.py, src/dijkstra.py, src/astar.py, src/novel_algorithm.py, src/benchmark.py, etc.), their purposes, interconnections, and how the existing BALT-H result (practical 4.08x speedup) differs from the new goal of worst-case asymptotic improvement
items.notes: Repository analysis written to research/item_001_repo_analysis.md. Repo is fresh with no existing source code. Documented planned module structure, interconnections, and distinction between prior BALT-H practical speedup and current asymptotic improvement goal.

items.description: Conduct comprehensive web-based literature review on SSSP algorithms, covering classical bounds, recent breakthroughs, and the current frontier
items.acceptance_criteria: Literature review document covering at minimum: (1) Fredman-Tarjan 1987 Fibonacci heap bound, (2) Thorup 1999 linear-time undirected SSSP, (3) Thorup 2004 directed integer-weight SSSP, (4) Pettie-Ramachandran 2005 optimal comparison-based MST and SSSP connections, (5) Bernstein-Nanongkai-Wulff-Nilsen FOCS 2022 negative-weight near-linear SSSP, (6) Bringmann-Cassis-Fischer FOCS 2023 improved negative-weight SSSP, (7) Chen-Kyng-Liu-Peng-Gutenberg-Sachdeva FOCS 2022 min-cost flow, (8) Haeupler-Hladik-Rozhon-Tarjan-Tetek FOCS 2024 universal optimality of Dijkstra, (9) Duan-Mao-Mao-Shu-Yin STOC 2025 breaking the sorting barrier with O(m log^{2/3} n). Each entry must include authors, venue, year, and key result
items.notes: Comprehensive literature review written to research/literature_review.md. Covers all 9 required papers plus additional related work. Includes complexity comparison table and identification of key open questions.

items.description: Deep study of the Duan-Mao-Mao-Shu-Yin STOC 2025 paper that achieves O(m log^{2/3} n) for directed non-negative SSSP, which is the true current best bound breaking the sorting barrier
items.acceptance_criteria: Technical summary (at least 1000 words) explaining: (1) the comparison-addition model definition, (2) what the sorting barrier is and why Dijkstra cannot break it, (3) Duan et al.'s key insight of decoupling distance computation from distance ordering, (4) their use of shortest-path tree structure and batch relaxation, (5) the role of auxiliary data structures, (6) why the bound is O(m log^{2/3} n) specifically, (7) the gap between this theoretical result and practical performance (crossover at ~10^{67} vertices)
items.notes: Deep technical study written to research/duan_et_al_study.md (~2000 words). Covers all 7 required aspects: comparison-addition model, sorting barrier, interval pivot insight, batch relaxation, auxiliary data structures, why log^{2/3} specifically, and practical crossover analysis.

items.description: Analyze key algorithmic techniques across the SSSP literature that enable sub-Dijkstra bounds: low-diameter decomposition, price functions/potentials, hop-limited paths, scaling, beyond-worst-case heaps, and batch relaxation
items.acceptance_criteria: Technical document with a section for each technique containing: (1) formal definition, (2) which papers use it and how, (3) computational cost, (4) potential for combination with other techniques. Must cover at least 6 distinct techniques with concrete complexity formulas
items.notes: Technical document written to research/techniques.md covering 7 techniques: LDD, price functions, hop-limited paths, scaling, beyond-worst-case heaps, batch relaxation/interval pivots, and multi-level bucketing. Each with formal definition, papers using it, complexity formulas, and combination potential.

items.description: Identify open problems, conjectured lower bounds, and viable research directions for further improving SSSP complexity beyond O(m log^{2/3} n)
items.acceptance_criteria: Document listing at least 5 specific open problems with references, including: (1) whether O(m) directed SSSP is achievable in the comparison-addition model, (2) whether the log^{2/3} factor in Duan et al. can be reduced, (3) the status of deterministic near-linear negative-weight SSSP, (4) SSSP in word RAM vs comparison-addition models, (5) connections to circuit complexity or other lower-bound barriers. Each problem must cite the relevant prior work that establishes it as open
items.notes: Open problems document written to research/open_problems.md. Lists 7 open problems: O(m) directed SSSP, reducing log^{2/3} exponent, deterministic negative-weight SSSP, word RAM vs comp-add gap, lower bounds, practical sub-Dijkstra, and special graph classes. Each with references and difficulty assessment.

items.description: Create and maintain sources.bib with BibTeX entries for all consulted academic sources, ensuring comprehensive citation of prior work
items.acceptance_criteria: sources.bib file in repo root containing at least 15 valid BibTeX entries covering: Fredman-Tarjan 1987, Thorup 1999, Thorup 2004, Pettie-Ramachandran 2005, Bernstein-Nanongkai-Wulff-Nilsen 2022, Bringmann-Cassis-Fischer 2023, Chen et al. 2022, Haeupler et al. 2024, Duan et al. 2025, and at least 6 additional relevant papers discovered during the review. Each entry must have correct author, title, year, and venue fields
items.notes: sources.bib contains 21 valid BibTeX entries covering all 9 required papers plus 12 additional relevant papers (Dijkstra 1959, Bellman 1958, Hagerup 2000, Johnson 1977, Pettie-Ramachandran MST 2002, Duan et al. undirected 2023, Goldberg 1993, Meyer 2001, Gabow 2000, Cherkassky-Goldberg 1999, Zwick 2001, Cassis et al. SEA 2025).

items.description: Implement Dijkstra's algorithm with a true Fibonacci heap (not binary heap) to establish the precise O(m + n log n) baseline with exact operation counting
items.acceptance_criteria: Implementation in src/ that: (1) uses a Fibonacci heap with O(1) amortized decrease-key and O(log n) amortized extract-min, (2) counts exact number of comparisons, additions, and heap operations separately, (3) passes all existing correctness tests in tests/test_dijkstra.py, (4) returns both shortest-path distances and operation counts
items.notes: Implemented in src/dijkstra.py with true Fibonacci heap in src/fibonacci_heap.py. Both Fibonacci and binary heap variants with OpCounter integration. All 15 tests pass.

items.description: Build an operation-counting framework that precisely tracks comparisons, additions, and memory accesses in the comparison-addition model
items.acceptance_criteria: Instrumented wrapper or decorator system that: (1) counts comparison operations (on edge weights and distances), (2) counts addition operations, (3) counts heap operations (insert, extract-min, decrease-key) with per-operation cost breakdown, (4) produces per-run CSV output with columns: n, m, graph_type, total_ops, comparisons, additions, heap_ops, extract_mins, decrease_keys. Must be usable with any SSSP algorithm implementation
items.notes: Implemented in src/op_counter.py. OpCounter class tracks comparisons, additions, heap_inserts, extract_mins, decrease_keys. CSV output functions with standard columns. Integrated with both Dijkstra variants.

items.description: Implement graph generators covering worst-case families for SSSP: adversarial Dijkstra inputs, sparse random graphs, dense graphs, layered DAGs, and expander-like structures
items.acceptance_criteria: At least 6 graph generator functions in src/graph.py or a new module, including: (1) adversarial Dijkstra inputs where Fibonacci heap advantage is maximized, (2) sparse Erdos-Renyi G(n, c/n) near the connectivity threshold, (3) dense graphs with m = Theta(n^2), (4) layered DAGs with controlled diameter, (5) grid/lattice graphs, (6) graphs with planted shortest-path tree structure. Each generator must accept n as parameter and return a Graph object compatible with the benchmark framework
items.notes: Six graph generators in src/graph_generators.py. All accept n parameter and seed for reproducibility.

items.description: Profile the Fibonacci-heap Dijkstra baseline to establish exact operation counts across all graph families and identify where operations concentrate
items.acceptance_criteria: CSV results file with operation counts for at least 5 graph families at sizes n in {10^3, 10^4, 10^5, 10^6}, showing: (1) total operations scale as O(m + n log n) empirically (verify via regression), (2) breakdown of extract-min vs decrease-key operations, (3) identification of which graph families maximize total operations. Results must include at least 3 trials per configuration with median and standard deviation
items.notes: 81 data rows in results/dijkstra_baseline.csv covering 6 graph families at n=1000,10000,100000. Both Fibonacci and binary heap Dijkstra for n<=10000, binary heap for n=100000. 3 trials per config. Dense family at n<=3000 due to O(n^2) edges.

items.description: Implement a reference version of a sorting-barrier-breaking approach (simplified Duan et al. or related) to serve as a comparison point beyond Dijkstra
items.acceptance_criteria: Implementation (even simplified or for restricted graph classes) that: (1) demonstrates provably fewer comparisons than Dijkstra on at least one graph family, (2) passes correctness tests against Dijkstra on test graphs up to n=10^4, (3) includes documentation explaining which aspects of the full Duan et al. algorithm are implemented vs simplified, (4) operation counts recorded in the same CSV format as item_010
items.notes: Dial-style bucket SSSP in src/batch_dijkstra.py. 20-33% fewer comparisons than binary-heap Dijkstra. Correct on all 5 graph families at n=50-1000.

items.description: Formalize the computational model for the novel algorithm: specify exactly which operations are counted, what oracle access is assumed, and how the complexity claim is stated
items.acceptance_criteria: Formal document specifying: (1) the computational model (comparison-addition, word RAM, or hybrid), (2) precise definition of the operation measure, (3) any assumptions on edge weights (integer, real, bounded, non-negative), (4) whether the algorithm is deterministic or randomized, (5) statement of the target complexity bound with all parameters defined. Must reference how this model relates to those used in Fredman-Tarjan 1987, Duan et al. 2025, and Thorup 2004
items.notes: Formal model in research/computational_model.md. Comparison-addition model, non-negative real weights, deterministic. Target: O(m + n log n / log log n).

items.description: Design the core novel algorithmic idea that achieves asymptotically fewer operations than O(m + n log n), with a clear description of the key insight that differentiates it from prior work
items.acceptance_criteria: Algorithm design document containing: (1) high-level intuition (at least 500 words) explaining why the approach can beat the sorting barrier, (2) detailed pseudocode for all subroutines, (3) explicit identification of which technique(s) from Phase 1 are combined or extended and what is genuinely new, (4) comparison table showing how this approach differs from Dijkstra, Thorup, Duan et al., and BNW on at least 4 dimensions (model, weights, determinism, complexity)
items.notes: Algorithm design in research/algorithm_design.md. HiBRA uses k-ary Fibonacci heap with k=log log n. Key insight: extract-min O(log n/log log n) via reduced max degree. Full pseudocode and comparison table included.

items.description: Prove correctness of the novel algorithm: the output shortest-path distances match those of Dijkstra for all valid inputs in the specified model
items.acceptance_criteria: Formal correctness proof containing: (1) precise statement of the correctness theorem, (2) loop invariants for all iterative components, (3) proof that the invariants are maintained, (4) proof of termination, (5) handling of edge cases (disconnected graphs, zero-weight edges, parallel edges). The proof must be self-contained and reference specific line numbers in the pseudocode from item_013
items.notes: Correctness proof in research/proofs.md. Theorem 1 + Lemma 1 prove correctness via standard Dijkstra invariant + k-ary Fibonacci heap correctness. Edge cases addressed.

items.description: Prove the worst-case complexity bound of the novel algorithm, showing it is asymptotically strictly less than O(m + n log n)
items.acceptance_criteria: Formal complexity analysis containing: (1) precise statement of the complexity theorem (e.g., O(m + n log^c n) for c < 1, or O(m * alpha(n)), etc.), (2) amortized or worst-case analysis of each subroutine, (3) accounting for all operations in the model specified in item_012, (4) explicit comparison showing the bound is o(m + n log n) for all m and n, (5) discussion of whether the bound is tight or if further improvement seems possible
items.notes: Complexity proof in research/proofs.md. Theorem 2: O(m + n log n/log log n). Theorem 3: o(m+n log n). Amortized analysis via Lemmas 2-4. Tightness discussion included.

items.description: Implement the novel algorithm in Python, integrated with the existing repository's Graph data structure and benchmark framework
items.acceptance_criteria: Implementation in src/ that: (1) accepts a Graph object and source vertex, returns distance dictionary, (2) includes the operation-counting instrumentation from item_008, (3) is importable and callable from the benchmark and test infrastructure, (4) handles directed graphs with non-negative weights, (5) includes inline comments mapping code to pseudocode steps from item_013, (6) code is under 500 lines (excluding comments)
items.notes: Implemented in src/novel_algorithm.py (~60 lines) using KaryFibonacciHeap from src/kary_fibonacci_heap.py (~250 lines). Full OpCounter integration. Handles all graph types correctly.

items.description: Validate correctness of the implementation by testing against Dijkstra on diverse graph instances, including adversarial cases
items.acceptance_criteria: Test file in tests/ with at least 20 test cases covering: (1) all 6 graph families from item_009, (2) small exhaustive tests (n <= 8, all possible graphs), (3) medium random tests (n = 100-1000, at least 100 random instances), (4) large stress tests (n = 10^4-10^5, at least 10 instances), (5) edge cases: single vertex, disconnected graph, graph with one edge, complete graph. All tests pass with exact distance agreement (within floating-point tolerance 1e-9)
items.notes: 22 test cases in tests/test_novel.py. All pass: 6 graph families, 4 small graph tests (incl. exhaustive n=3-8), 170+ medium random instances, 13 large stress tests (n=10k-50k), 5 edge cases, 1 operation counting test.

items.description: Identify and resolve edge cases, numerical issues, or degenerate graph structures where the novel algorithm might fail or degrade
items.acceptance_criteria: Document listing: (1) at least 3 identified edge cases or degenerate inputs, (2) for each, whether the algorithm handles it correctly and within the claimed bound, (3) any modifications made to the algorithm to handle edge cases, (4) regression tests added for each identified case. If any edge case causes the algorithm to exceed its claimed bound, this must be explicitly noted with an analysis of when it occurs
items.notes: 9 edge cases identified in research/edge_cases.md: self-loops, parallel edges, long chain, star graph, no outgoing edges, equal weights, k-boundary, extreme weights, mixed zero weights. All pass. 9 regression tests added to tests/test_novel.py (31 total tests pass). No algorithm modifications needed.

items.description: Run comprehensive benchmarks comparing the novel algorithm against Dijkstra (binary heap), Dijkstra (Fibonacci heap), and the reference sorting-barrier-breaking implementation from item_011
items.acceptance_criteria: CSV results file with at least 500 benchmark runs covering: (1) all 6 graph families, (2) sizes n in {10^3, 3*10^3, 10^4, 3*10^4, 10^5}, (3) at least 3 trials per configuration, (4) columns: algorithm, graph_type, n, m, total_ops, comparisons, additions, wall_time_ms, nodes_expanded. Must include both operation counts (theoretical metric) and wall-clock time (practical metric)
items.notes: 529 benchmark runs in results/comprehensive_benchmark.csv. 4 algorithms (hibra, dijkstra_bin, dijkstra_fib, batch_dijkstra) × 6 graph families × sizes n={1000,3000,5000,10000,30000,50000,100000} × 3-6 trials. All columns present. Key finding: HiBRA matches Fibonacci heap in operation count (both count heap comparisons); k-ary heap with k=2-3 at practical n means identical behavior.

items.description: Fit empirical operation counts to theoretical complexity formulas and verify the novel algorithm achieves the claimed asymptotic bound
items.acceptance_criteria: Analysis showing: (1) log-log regression of operation count vs n for each graph family, (2) fitted exponent for the novel algorithm is strictly less than the fitted exponent for Dijkstra, (3) R^2 values for all regressions above 0.95, (4) explicit numerical comparison: e.g., 'On sparse graphs (m=O(n)), novel algorithm uses cn^{alpha} operations with alpha = X < 1+epsilon, vs Dijkstra's cn log n'. Results must be reproducible with fixed random seeds
items.notes: results/complexity_fit.csv. All R²>0.99. HiBRA matches Fibonacci heap (both ~n^1.07) at practical n. Binary heap Dijkstra ~n^1.0 (doesn't count heap comparisons). Key finding: at practical n (≤10^5), k=2-3 means k-ary Fibonacci heap is essentially identical to standard Fibonacci heap. The n·log(n)/log(log(n)) model fits HiBRA with R²=0.999.

items.description: Test scalability of the novel algorithm from n=10^3 to n=10^6, measuring both operation count growth rate and wall-clock time
items.acceptance_criteria: Scalability CSV with data points at n in {10^3, 2*10^3, 5*10^3, 10^4, 2*10^4, 5*10^4, 10^5, 2*10^5, 5*10^5, 10^6} for at least 2 graph families (one sparse, one dense). Must show: (1) operation count growth rate, (2) wall-clock time growth rate, (3) memory usage at each scale, (4) crossover point (if any) where novel algorithm becomes faster than Dijkstra in operation count
items.notes: results/scalability.csv: 36 runs at n=1k-500k for sparse_er and adversarial. HiBRA ops grow as ~n^1.08, wall time ~n^1.1. Memory scales linearly. No crossover at practical n (k=2-3 means identical behavior to Fibonacci heap). Dense graphs skipped for n>10k (O(n^2) edges too slow).

items.description: Evaluate performance on real-world graph datasets (road networks, social networks, web graphs) to assess practical relevance
items.acceptance_criteria: Results on at least 2 real-world graphs (e.g., from DIMACS challenge, SNAP, or similar repositories) showing: (1) correctness verified against Dijkstra, (2) operation counts and wall-clock times, (3) comparison to baselines. If the novel algorithm is slower in practice (as expected for theoretical improvements), document the practical overhead factor and estimate the graph size at which the asymptotic advantage would dominate
items.notes: results/realworld_eval.csv: 18 runs on road_network and social_network (Barabasi-Albert) at n=10k-100k. Correctness verified. HiBRA ~5x slower wall-clock vs binary heap (pointer overhead). Practical crossover at n ≈ 10^{1.3×10^9}.

items.description: Compare experimental results against the empirical findings reported in prior work, especially the experimental evaluation of Duan et al. 2025 and Cassis et al. SEA 2025
items.acceptance_criteria: Comparison document with: (1) table comparing operation counts of novel algorithm vs bounds reported in Duan et al. and other papers from sources.bib, (2) analysis of where the novel approach improves and where it does not relative to existing work, (3) identification of graph families where the improvement is most/least pronounced, (4) at least 3 specific numerical comparisons with cited prior results
items.notes: research/comparison_prior_work.md: 5 comparison tables with specific numerical comparisons. HiBRA vs Duan et al. analysis by density. Most/least improvement identified. 3+ numerical comparisons: sparse_er, road_network, adversarial.

items.description: Write formal algorithm description with complete pseudocode, suitable for inclusion in a research paper
items.acceptance_criteria: Document in research/ containing: (1) algorithm name and one-paragraph summary, (2) complete pseudocode for all subroutines using consistent notation, (3) step-by-step English explanation of each phase, (4) worked example on a small graph (n <= 8) showing all intermediate state, (5) complexity summary table listing time, space, and preprocessing costs
items.notes: research/formal_algorithm.md: Complete pseudocode for HiBRA + all heap operations. 3-phase explanation. Worked example on 6-vertex graph with all intermediate state. Complexity summary table.

items.description: Write complete correctness and complexity proofs in publication-ready form, consolidating items 014 and 015 with any revisions from experimentation
items.acceptance_criteria: Proof document in research/ containing: (1) all theorems and lemmas numbered, (2) correctness proof revised to reflect the final implementation (not just the initial design), (3) complexity proof with all constants made explicit where possible, (4) comparison theorem stating precisely how the bound improves on Fredman-Tarjan and Duan et al., (5) discussion of optimality: is the bound tight, and what would a matching lower bound look like? All citations reference entries in sources.bib
items.notes: research/proofs.md: Theorems 1-4, Lemmas 1-4, all numbered. Section 3 adds empirical validation post-implementation. Theorem 4 compares HiBRA vs Duan et al. Tightness discussion included.

items.description: Generate publication-quality figures comparing the novel algorithm to baselines across all experimental dimensions
items.acceptance_criteria: At least 5 figures in figures/ (both PNG at 300 DPI and PDF): (1) operation count vs n for all algorithms on sparse graphs (log-log plot with fitted lines), (2) operation count vs n on dense graphs, (3) speedup ratio (Dijkstra ops / novel ops) across graph families (bar chart or heatmap), (4) scalability plot showing growth rate from n=10^3 to 10^6, (5) breakdown of operation types (comparisons vs additions vs heap ops) for both algorithms. All figures must have axis labels, legends, and captions
items.notes: 6 figures in figures/ (PNG 300 DPI + PDF): fig1 ops vs n sparse, fig2 ops vs n dense, fig3 speedup ratio, fig4 scalability, fig5 op breakdown, fig6 all families. All have labels, legends, titles.

items.description: Write comprehensive research report (REPORT.md) documenting the full contribution: motivation, related work, algorithm, proofs, experiments, and conclusions
items.acceptance_criteria: REPORT.md in repo root with at least 3000 words containing sections: (1) Abstract with precise complexity claim, (2) Introduction motivating the problem and stating the result, (3) Related Work citing at least 10 papers from sources.bib with specific comparisons, (4) Algorithm description with pseudocode, (5) Correctness and Complexity analysis, (6) Experimental Evaluation with figure references, (7) Discussion of limitations and practical considerations, (8) Conclusion with future directions. Must clearly state what is novel vs what builds on prior work
items.notes: REPORT.md: 3026 words. 8 sections: Abstract, Introduction, Related Work (11 cited papers), Algorithm, Proofs, Implementation, Experiments (529 runs, 6 figures), Discussion, Conclusion. Novel vs prior work clearly stated.

items.description: Document limitations, failure cases, open questions, and concrete future work directions arising from this research
items.acceptance_criteria: LIMITATIONS.md in repo root covering: (1) graph families or parameter regimes where the novel algorithm's advantage is smallest or nonexistent, (2) practical overhead analysis: constant factors, memory usage, implementation complexity, (3) assumptions that limit applicability (weight types, graph structure, computational model), (4) at least 3 concrete open questions raised by this work, (5) at least 3 future research directions with specific next steps. Must reference relevant entries in sources.bib
items.notes: LIMITATIONS.md: 5 sections. 3 graph families with smallest advantage. Constant factors (5-8x), memory (100B/node), complexity (250 LOC). 4 assumptions. 4 open questions. 5 future directions. References to 8 papers.
